Create worktree /opt/nxeon-wt-seamless on new branch feature/seamless-promote from current main (`git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /opt/nxeon-wt-seamless -b feature/seamless-promote main`; verify pwd before each command).

PROBLEM (owner request): scripts/promote-production.sh runs `npm run build` INSIDE /opt/nxeon, which wipes/rewrites /opt/nxeon/.next while the live service (systemd nxeon-web = `node .next/standalone/server.js`, WorkingDirectory /opt/nxeon) is still serving from it. Result today (2026-10-01): for 10-12 minutes per promote the site returned HTML but /_next/static/* chunks returned 400, lazy routes broke, .next/standalone/server.js was missing; a hung `next build` (11 min at ~1% CPU) left prod half-dead; two concurrent promotes collided (ENOTEMPTY .next/export). The owner wants deploys to be SEAMLESS: building must never affect the live app.

DESIGN GOAL: (1) build in a SEPARATE directory (e.g. /opt/nxeon-build, a git worktree or checkout of the target ref with the PRODUCTION .env copied in so NEXT_PUBLIC_* / build-time env are correct for prod — verify that staging's different .env is not reused; node_modules installed there); (2) run all the existing post-build steps there (geoip data copy, .next/static + public copy into standalone, chown for the non-root web user — read the current promote script and keep EVERY step it does); (3) put the finished standalone output in a release dir /opt/nxeon-releases/<BUILD_ID>/ and cut over with the smallest possible window: e.g. rsync/cp into place, atomically swap (rename) so /opt/nxeon/.next is replaced in one `mv` and then `systemctl restart nxeon-web` (downtime = restart seconds), WITHOUT needing to edit systemd unit files (the harness blocks edits under /etc/systemd — design around that; if a symlink-based release is only possible with a unit change, propose it as an optional phase 2 with the exact unit diff but make phase 1 work without it); verify the new build serves (HTTP 200 on / and a real /_next/static chunk) BEFORE declaring success and auto-rollback to the previous release if the health check fails; keep the last 3 releases for instant rollback (and a rollback script); (4) keep today's other safety behaviour: prisma generate + additive `db push` ordering (do these BEFORE the swap but make sure `prisma generate` in /opt/nxeon cannot ever bake the wrong .env/DB path), wait for in-flight PROVISION jobs before restarting the worker (D1's drain already makes restarts safe; keep the existing wait logic, but never let it delay the web cutover — restart web first, worker after), copy deploy/*.service only if changed and just print instructions for it if it cannot be done; (5) safety: flock so two promotes can never run at once, a build timeout (kill the build tree if no progress for N minutes or total > 20 min), run the build with nice/ionice, refuse to start when available memory < a threshold, never leave /opt/nxeon/.next in a partial state; (6) dry-run mode (`--dry-run`) that does everything except the swap/restart; (7) ALSO fix scripts/deploy-staging.sh the same way if it can break the staging app while building. TEST thoroughly WITHOUT touching prod: exercise the swap/rollback/health-check logic against the STAGING app (nxeon-staging-web service, /opt/nxeon-staging, port 3001 — check how it is wired) or a throwaway copy on another port, including a forced failing health check to prove auto-rollback, and a simulated hung build to prove the timeout; measure the real downtime window while curling in a loop during a staging cutover and report the number. Do not run it against production. Update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md and the memory-note text in /root/FLEET-STATUS-2026-10-01.md (section 'OWNER REQUEST ... seamless production deploys') with how to use it. Commit with explicit paths on your branch, write /root/agent-notes/seamless.md, and report: what changed, measured downtime, what was verified vs not, and the exact owner steps to adopt it (including anything the harness will block).

# Nxeon agent brief — READ FULLY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING

You are one of ~20 agents working IN PARALLEL on the Nxeon platform (a Hostinger-style VPS + game-server hosting business).
This machine IS the live production primary. Real paying customers are on it right now. Be careful, be thorough, be honest.

## Orientation (do this first, ~5 min)
- Read `/opt/nxeon/CLAUDE.md` (architecture, design-system scoping rules, conventions) and the parts of `/opt/nxeon/docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` relevant to your task.
- Stack: Next.js 15 App Router + TS + Tailwind v4 + Prisma 6 + Postgres 17; worker = `worker/index.ts` (systemd `nxeon-worker`); Proxmox across 5 non-clustered nodes (primary + node-2..5, each its own NAT island 10.20.N.0/24).
- Two portals: admin (`app/admin/**`, shell `components/portal/Shell.tsx`, ORIGINAL chrome) and customer (`app/dashboard/**`, shell `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, "Nexion" redesign). Marketing: `app/nxm/**` (NEW, generated partly by `tools/nxm` — change the generators, not generated output) + legacy `app/(marketing)/**`.
- Already done TODAY on main (don't redo): worker concurrency (WORKER_CONCURRENCY=8 + per-server lock), ServerMemSample guest-memory fix, Minecraft/Valheim/Terraria power-start timeout 180s, creator-outreach CSV queue (OutreachQueueItem, worker `processOutreachQueueTick`, `lib/creator-outreach-send-core.ts`), admin invite preview now matches the sent template, geoip/static postbuild.

## HARD RULES (non-negotiable)
1. **Worktree only.** `git -C /opt/nxeon worktree add /opt/nxeon-wt-<short> -b <type>/<short> main`. NEVER edit files under `/opt/nxeon` itself. NEVER run, anywhere: `npm run build`/`next build` in `/opt/nxeon`, `systemctl restart|stop` on nxeon services, `prisma db push` against the prod DB, `git merge`/`git push`/`git checkout` in `/opt/nxeon`, `scripts/promote-production.sh`, `scripts/deploy-staging.sh`. The main thread merges and deploys. Your deliverable is committed work on your own branch + a report.
2. **node_modules**: symlink per-entry so you can still get an isolated Prisma client:
   `mkdir node_modules && for f in /opt/nxeon/node_modules/* /opt/nxeon/node_modules/.[!.]*; do b=$(basename $f); case $b in @prisma|.prisma) continue;; esac; ln -s $f node_modules/$b; done; cp -r /opt/nxeon/node_modules/@prisma node_modules/@prisma; cp -r /opt/nxeon/node_modules/.prisma node_modules/.prisma`
   Then `npx prisma generate` only touches YOUR copy. NEVER run `prisma generate` against the shared `/opt/nxeon/node_modules` (it would change production's client).
3. **Heavy commands** (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) MUST go through the global lock: `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-<short> && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."`. Never start more than one dev server; kill it when done. Do not run `next build` at all (CLAUDE.md allows it locally but 20 parallel builds would take production down) — typecheck + real dev-server renders are your verification.
4. **Running the app / schema changes**: use a throwaway database: `sudo -u postgres createdb nxeon_agt_<short>` then `DATABASE_URL=postgresql:///nxeon_agt_<short>?host=/var/run/postgresql npx prisma db push` (additive schema only; drop it when finished). Use `NXEON_SANDBOX=1`, your assigned PORT, and a temporary `.env` (copy `/opt/nxeon/.env` values you need, but override DATABASE_URL and set NXEON_SANDBOX=1). Remove `.env` before committing. Read-only queries against the prod DB (via `/opt/nxeon/.env`) are fine for diagnosis; prod writes are forbidden unless your task text explicitly allows a specific one.
5. **Never touch customers**: no provisioning/stopping/restarting real customer VMs or containers, no DNS/Stripe/email sends, no real emails to anyone. Read-only SSH diagnosis of nodes/guests is fine. If your task explicitly allows live test VMs, follow its limits exactly (dedicated test account, never the primary node, ≤2 concurrent, tear down after, brand-new VMIDs only — never reuse an ID, check all 5 nodes).
6. **If a command is denied by the auto-mode classifier, do not work around it** — record it in your report as "needs owner to run" with the exact command.
7. **Git**: commit small and often with explicit paths — NEVER `git add -A` / `git add .` (symlinked worktrees can corrupt prod). Never commit `.env`, secrets, scratch files. Write commit messages to a file and use `git commit -F file` (backticks break `-m`). End messages with `Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>`. A post-commit hook auto-pushes your branch to GitHub; that is expected.
8. **Docs**: update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` (§15 change history + any affected section) in the same commits (repo rule). Do not run publish-docs.
9. **Security for anything admin/ops**: gate with `requireArea(...)`/`requireAdmin()`, write `AuditLog`, confirm destructive actions, make them idempotent, run long/remote work as `Job` rows (web app never mutates Proxmox directly), validate every value that reaches a shell with shell-inert allowlists (see `lib/ssh-exec.ts`), never log secrets/passwords/tokens.
10. **Product/brand rules**: Nxeon speaks as the owner — never mention third-party infrastructure providers (OVH/Hetzner/"our provider") in customer-facing text. Never fabricate stats, reviews, player counts, ETAs — if a number can't come from the DB or a real upstream, leave it empty. "47 seconds" is an intentional brand tagline, leave it. First-month-free promo is HOSTING-ONLY. "What's New" announcements are customer-facing changes only. Visual language: dark navy + violet→blue gradient (#3b6be8→#7b3fef) + cyan accents; study `app/nxm` (marketing) and `components/nx` (customer portal) and match them.
11. Respect other agents: ownership map below. Edit outside your area ONLY for minimal, clearly necessary hook-ups, and list each such file in your report so the integrator can resolve conflicts. Pull `main` into your branch (`git merge main` in your worktree) near the end if main moved.
12. Quality bar: real verification. Typecheck must be clean. For UI, actually render it (Playwright against your dev server, screenshots at mobile+desktop, light+dark where relevant) and look at the result. For logic, write/run tests or scripts that exercise it. Say honestly what you did NOT verify.

## Ownership map (who edits what)
- R gamestate: game status truth, GAME_CONFIG/power semantics, auto-update toggle, post-provision reachability (`worker/game-control.ts`, `worker/game-config.ts`, `worker/game-update.ts`, game panel status/power UI)
- D1 concur: worker loop/queue/concurrency/latency, SSH node targeting (`worker/index.ts` loop, `lib/sftp.ts`, `lib/ssh-exec.ts`, sweeps)
- D2 provspeed: provisioning scripts + speed (`prisma/catalog.ts`, `prisma/seed-*`, `provision()` in worker/index.ts), golden templates
- P audit: read-only audit + small clear fixes + `docs/AUDIT-*.md`
- Q nodedocs: `scripts/onboard-node.sh`, `scripts/verify-node.sh`, node docs
- A1 adminshell: admin shell/IA/nav/redesign (`components/admin/shell/*`, `lib/admin-nav.ts`, `app/admin/layout*`, admin dashboard home)
- A2 adminops: `app/admin/ops/**`, `lib/admin-ops/**`, `worker/admin-ops.ts`, `components/admin/ops/*`
- A3 insights: `app/admin/insights/**`, `lib/insights/**`, bot filtering in visitor analytics (`worker/analytics.ts`, visitor tracking libs)
- B adminmail: `app/admin/mail/**`, `components/customer/mail/**` (shared with the customer Business Email product — don't break it), `lib/actions-mail.ts`, `lib/mail/**`
- C outreach: `app/admin/partners/**`, outreach/partner libs, partner game-server grants
- F freemc: free Minecraft (`lib/free-minecraft-*`, `lib/actions-free-minecraft.ts`, `components/customer/freemc/*`)
- L freevalheim: new free Valheim modules + directory + marketing pages
- K1 modinstall: per-game mod INSTALL mechanics + Mods tab; K2 modcatalog: catalog ingestion/mirror/auto-update (owns Mod schema)
- H tours: `components/nx/tour/*`, `lib/tours/*`, `data-tour` attributes (minimal) in dashboards
- I1 nxlabs: customer-portal NX Labs pages + preloader
- I2 portalmobile: customer-portal responsiveness (everything except NX Labs/preloader)
- J mktpolish: marketing footer/promo bar/nav + marketing responsiveness
- M skins: Minecraft skin creator (marketing tool page + customer tools)
- N seo: SEO across static/marketing pages, SEO audit tooling

## Final report (your last message) — under 400 words
Branch + worktree path + commit list; what changed (by file/area); how you verified (commands/screenshots); schema changes (models/fields added — additive?); files edited outside your area; anything blocked / needs owner action (exact commands); risks and follow-ups. Be blunt about what's incomplete.

Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

#!/bin/bash
# Promote the currently deployed staging commit to production.
# Verifies staging is healthy, fast-forwards nothing (prod working tree IS the repo),
# then rebuilds + restarts production services.
set -euo pipefail

STG_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon-staging rev-parse HEAD)
PROD_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon rev-parse HEAD)

echo "==> Staging is at:    $STG_COMMIT"
echo "==> Production is at: $PROD_COMMIT"

if ! systemctl is-active -q nxeon-staging-web; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging web service is not running." >&2
  exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
if [ "$CODE" != "200" ]; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging returns HTTP $CODE." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ "$STG_COMMIT" != "$PROD_COMMIT" ]; then
  echo "Note: production tree is at a different commit than staging."
  echo "Production deploys directly from /opt/nxeon's working tree (main)."
fi

cd /opt/nxeon
echo "==> Installing dependencies (adds any new deps before build)"
# CRITICAL: without this, a commit that adds a new dependency (e.g. imapflow)
# builds against a stale node_modules and fails — which previously aborted the
# promote AFTER the old build was already gone. Always sync deps first.
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -3
# CRITICAL: this was previously `prisma generate` only — regenerates the
# CLIENT's types (fixes the build) but never touches the actual DATABASE.
# Staging and production are SEPARATE databases (nxeon_staging vs nxeon, same
# Postgres server, confirmed live) — deploy-staging.sh's own `db push` only
# ever applies to staging's DB, so a schema change promoted this way built
# and deployed fine while production's actual table never got the new
# column, silently breaking the FIRST thing that queried it post-deploy
# (found live 2026-09-02: worker/billing.ts's sweeps started throwing
# "column does not exist" immediately after a routine promote — no staging
# failure gave any warning, since staging's own db push had already
# succeeded there). `db push` both applies the schema AND regenerates the
# client, so this replaces the old generate-only step rather than adding a
# second one. Schema changes are rare enough that this always running
# unconditionally costs nothing when there's nothing new to push.
echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --schema=/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma 2>&1 | tail -4
echo "==> Building production"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4
# Guard: never restart into an incomplete/failed build. A valid production build
# always writes .next/BUILD_ID; if it's missing the build failed mid-way and the
# old in-memory process is still serving — abort rather than kill it.
if [ ! -s /opt/nxeon/.next/BUILD_ID ]; then
  echo "BUILD FAILED: .next/BUILD_ID missing — NOT restarting (old process left serving)." >&2
  exit 1
fi
# next.config sets output:"standalone"; the standalone server.js is what the
# systemd unit actually runs (not `next start` — see deploy-staging.sh's own
# comment on this same step for the 2026-09-10 incident). Its output does NOT
# include public/ or .next/static/ (Next's documented behavior) — refresh
# them every promote, same as staging, or new/changed static assets are
# missing from prod until the next promote happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle since it reads .dat files off its own package path at runtime) — the
# standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace as JS-imported, so
# an externalized package's own non-JS data files are silently left behind.
# Found live 2026-09-10 on staging: this crashes EVERY request with an
# uncaught ENOENT the moment something runs the standalone server.js instead
# of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around geoip.lookup() does NOT
# help, the failure isn't confined to that call. Copy the real data/
# directory every promote, same reasoning as public/.next/static above. This
# has NOT yet bitten production because nxeon-web's systemd unit still runs
# `npm start` (next start) today, not server.js directly — but this fix must
# land before that switch happens, not after.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi
# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. .next needs to be writable by it
# (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable. .env is the one
# exception: systemd's EnvironmentFile= reads it as root (PID 1, pre-privilege
# drop) so the app's process env is fine either way, but Prisma's generated
# client ALSO opens .env directly at Client instantiation to resolve its own
# env() directives — that read happens as the actual 'nxeon' process user, so
# a root-owned .env throws EACCES there on every cold start (harmless once
# systemd's injected vars are already in process.env, but noisy, and a prior
# root-run edit to this file silently reverted the ownership fix below once
# already — confirmed live 2026-09-02). Keep .env nxeon-owned, not world- or
# group-readable. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next/.env ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chown nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
echo "==> Restarting production web"
systemctl restart nxeon-web

# Drain in-flight provisions before bouncing the worker. Restarting the worker
# mid-provision used to interrupt a live VM build and (with a non-idempotent retry)
# strand the server in ERROR. The start step is now idempotent so this is
# belt-and-suspenders, but avoiding the interruption entirely is cleaner. Bounded
# wait (max ~4 min) so a deploy can never hang forever.
DBURL=$(grep -E '^DATABASE_URL=' /opt/nxeon/.env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2- | tr -d '"')
if [ -n "$DBURL" ] && command -v psql >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  for _ in $(seq 1 24); do
    ACTIVE=$(psql "$DBURL" -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM \"Job\" WHERE status='RUNNING' AND type='PROVISION';" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]')
    [ "${ACTIVE:-0}" = "0" ] && break
    echo "==> Waiting for ${ACTIVE} in-flight provision(s) to finish before restarting worker…"
    sleep 10
  done
fi

echo "==> Restarting production worker"
systemctl restart nxeon-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-web nxeon-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1/)
echo "==> Production responds: HTTP $CODE"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "PRODUCTION UNHEALTHY — check journalctl -u nxeon-web"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Production promote complete"

# public/ or .next/static/ (Next's own documented behavior) — copy them in
# fresh every build, or every static asset/route added after the last copy
# is missing until the next deploy happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle on purpose, since it reads .dat files off its own package path at
# runtime) — but the standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace
# as JS-imported, so an externalized package's own non-JS data files are
# silently left behind. Found live 2026-09-10: this crashed EVERY request
# with an uncaught ENOENT the moment the systemd unit ran the standalone
# server.js instead of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around
# geoip.lookup() does NOT help, because the failure isn't confined to that
# call. Copy the package's real data/ directory in every build, same
# reasoning as public/.next/static above.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"

#!/bin/bash
# Three things (see 3. at the bottom) `next build` with output:"standalone" never does on its own —
# both confirmed live 2026-10-01 to take the whole site down when missed:
#
# 1. geoip-lite loads its .dat files off its own on-disk path at runtime
#    (not a statically-traceable require), so Next's standalone output
#    tracer misses them entirely — every request 500'd.

# future build/deploy can reintroduce either outage.

  mkdir -p ".next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite"
  cp -r "node_modules/geoip-lite/data" ".next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data"

fi

if [ -d ".next/static" ] && [ -d ".next/standalone/.next" ]; then
  rm -rf ".next/standalone/.next/static"
  cp -r ".next/static" ".next/standalone/.next/static"
  echo "[postbuild] copied .next/static into standalone output"
fi

#    copied into the standalone output (same documented Next.js behaviour).
#    scripts/promote-production.sh copies it, but any other build path
#    (a hand-run `npm run build && systemctl restart`) did not — and from that
#    restart until the next promote, EVERY public asset answered HTTP 400 on
#    every host. Confirmed in the nginx forensic log for 2026-10-01
#    02:54–03:10 UTC: 149/149 uncached image requests on the admin host and
#    all on the main host 400'd, then went back to 200 at the 03:10 promote.
#    This is the "none of the admin portal's images populate" report — the
#    admin is simply where the owner was looking during those windows.
if [ -d "public" ] && [ -d ".next/standalone" ]; then
  rm -rf ".next/standalone/public"
  cp -r "public" ".next/standalone/public"
  echo "[postbuild] copied public/ into standalone output"
fi

/**
 * Refuse to write to a database nobody deliberately pointed us at.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * THE INCIDENT THIS EXISTS FOR (2026-07-26)
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * An agent ran `prisma/seed.ts` from a scratch working tree. That tree had its
 * `node_modules` SYMLINKED to /opt/nxeon/node_modules, so `@prisma/client`
 * resolved through the symlink, and Prisma's dotenv loader walked up from the
 * REAL module location and loaded `/opt/nxeon/.env` — the PRODUCTION env. The
 * seed therefore connected to the production database `nxeon` while every human
 * signal (the cwd, the checkout, the intent) said "scratch".
 *
 * It happened to be a pure `upsert` seed, so it did no damage. That is luck, not
 * a control. The same accident with `prisma db push --accept-data-loss`, or with
 * a seed that had grown a `deleteMany`, destroys a live hosting platform's
 * customer records.
 *
 * The root cause is NOT "the seed was careless". It is that a writing script
 * inherits its target from ambient environment resolution — a mechanism with no
 * confirmation step, which resolves silently and can be wrong for reasons that
 * are invisible at the call site (a symlink three directories away).
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * THE CONTROL
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * A writing script must state, out loud, which database it believes it is about
 * to write to. The operator states it independently, via `NXEON_DB_TARGET`. The
 * script runs only if the two agree.
 *
 *     NXEON_DB_TARGET=nxeon_staging npx tsx prisma/seed.ts
 *
 * This is deliberately NOT a "--force"/"--yes" flag. A blanket confirmation
 * answers "do you want to proceed?", and in the incident above the honest answer
 * was yes — the operator did want to seed, just not THAT database. Naming the
 * target answers the question that was actually wrong. An operator who types
 * `NXEON_DB_TARGET=nxeon_scratch` while the environment silently resolves to
 * `nxeon` gets a refusal and a diff, which is exactly the moment the symlink
 * becomes visible.
 *
 * Pure and side-effect free so it can be unit-tested without a database; see
 * test/db-target-guard.test.ts.
 */

Now I'm sketching the overall architecture: a shared library script with reusable functions, parameterized by app directory, service names, port, build/release directories, env file, and build command, with a mode to deploy from a prebuilt release directory for testing and rollback — plus thin wrapper scripts for staging deploy, production promote, and rollback that just supply the right config to the shared library.

Within the library I'm defining a locking mechanism using flock to prevent concurrent promotions, a preflight check that verifies available memory and disk space before building, and a function to prepare the build tree as a git worktree for the given commit.

For existing worktrees, I'm detaching to the target commit and cleaning untracked files while preserving ignored directories like node_modules and .next cache. I want to keep the Next.js build cache for incremental speed while clearing stale build artifacts, so I'm removing everything in .next except the cache directory.

I'm also checking whether using a git worktree for the build dir writes correctly into the main repo's .git metadata, and whether any post-checkout hooks exist that might interfere. But I need to verify instrumentation.ts doesn't trigger side effects like background timers or emails if a second instance briefly runs during preflight — if it does, I'll either skip the preflight or disable it via an env var. For cutover, I'm planning an atomic symlink swap: point an incoming symlink at the new release, then move it into place over the existing .next symlink.

After restarting the web service, I'll do a health check — polling the root URL for up to 90 seconds expecting a success status, then confirming the first static JS chunk referenced in the HTML loads correctly, and checking that the build manifest files exist, since those are always generated regardless of app-router vs pages-router.

I should also verify through nginx that the correct build is being served, using a configurable secondary URL check for production. If the health check fails, I need a rollback path that restores the previous release symlink or swaps the legacy directory back, restarts, and re-verifies, failing loudly if that doesn't work either. Once the web cutover succeeds, I still need to handle the worker side — running npm install in the app directory since the worker depends on new packages and its own Prisma client.

Running prisma generate with a clean environment and explicit schema path, since generate doesn't need DATABASE_URL but I want to be certain it never picks up a stale env file. Then I should confirm the generated client's schema hash matches what was used in the build, and double-check that the app directory's HEAD commit hasn't drifted since the build started — otherwise the worker could end up running newer source than the web process.

I'm also weighing whether running npm install directly against the live directory while the old worker is still active poses any real risk beyond what already happens today — order relative to db push doesn't seem to matter much, and since the web build uses its own standalone node_modules, the old directory's install shouldn't interfere, including for things like the geoip data copy which now comes from the build directory. For the worker restart, I'll keep the existing drain-wait loop and active-state check. For deploy units, I want to diff the repo's service and timer files against what's installed in systemd and print the differences, applying them automatically if an install-units flag is set. Then I still need to handle pruning old releases, deciding how many to keep.

I'm settling on keeping the current release plus the three before it, making sure never to delete the current release or whatever the rollback target would be. For the legacy directory from earlier promotions, I only need it until there's at least one proper release to roll back to, so I can strip its cache directory right after a successful promote to free up disk space, since rollback only needs the standalone build, and it's safe to do this once the old process has already stopped.

For dry-run mode, I want it to skip any actual database mutation — instead of running `prisma db push`, it should run `prisma migrate diff` against the live schema to show the SQL that would apply without touching anything. Dry-run should still build and stage the release but mark it undeployed, and skip the install/generate steps and worker restart. I'm also planning a `--release <id>` flag for promote so it can redeploy an existing release, which the rollback script will reuse via a shared cutover function, and I'm sketching out the rollback script's interface now.

Rollback only applies to web since the worker runs from source and can't be rolled back without git, and schema changes stay forward-only since they're additive. Writing the watchdog logic...

I'm deciding to include cutime/cstime so CPU time from dead children still counts, and I need to parse /proc stat carefully since command names can contain parentheses or spaces. I'm also working through how setsid behaves when backgrounding a command inside a non-interactive script, since without job control the process may not already be its own group leader.

I should verify the resulting pgid matches $! to confirm setsid worked as expected, and separately I want to check actual build timings from the staging cache timestamps to calibrate a reasonable timeout instead of assuming the default 20 minutes.

With a 47,000-URL sitemap the build is probably 5-8 minutes, so I'll set a configurable max like BUILD_MAX_MIN rather than hardcoding. I should also lower process priority with nice/ionice, and still need to check instrumentation.ts along with root env settings like NODE_OPTIONS and any git hooks.

## Environments — production, staging, and the .env contract

The code is byte-identical between environments. Every difference is an environment variable. That
is the entire isolation model, which is why one wrong value in `.env` is how staging would eat
production's IP pool.

| | Production | Staging |
|---|---|---|
| Tree | `/opt/nxeon` | `/opt/nxeon-staging` |
| Database | `nxeon` | `nxeon_staging` |
| Web service | `nxeon-web.service` :3000 | `nxeon-staging-web.service` :3001 |
| Worker | `nxeon-worker.service` | `nxeon-staging-worker.service` |
| Terminal backend | `nxeon-terminal.service` | `nxeon-terminal-staging.service` |
| Console proxy | `nxeon-console-proxy.service` | `nxeon-staging-console-proxy.service` |
| VM IP pool | `10.20.0.100–250` | `10.20.0.50–99` |
| SSH DNAT ports | `20000–29999` | `30000–30999` |
| iptables chain | `NXEON_FWD` | `NXEON_FWD_STG` |
| Proxmox VM tag | *(none)* | `nxeon-staging` |
| Admin credentials | `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt` | `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt` |

The variables that create the split: `NXEON_ENV`, `NXEON_COOKIE_NAME`, `NXEON_NAT_CHAIN`,
`NXEON_TAG`, `NXEON_IP_START`, `NXEON_IP_END`, `NXEON_SSH_PORT_START`, `NXEON_SSH_PORT_END`,
`NXEON_CRED_FILE`, `PORT`, `APP_URL`.

**They share one Proxmox node and one ZFS pool.** Nothing but those ranges keeps them apart. Never
point staging pools at production ranges, and never `qm destroy` anything that has a `Server` row.

⚠ **Staging is not currently a faithful rehearsal environment, and this has already cost a
release.** Two separate kinds of drift:

- **The database is behind the tree.** `/opt/nxeon-staging/prisma/schema.prisma` has the card
  columns (`:147-148`) and `Invoice.stripePaymentIntentId` (`:466`); `nxeon_staging` has neither.
  `/dashboard/billing` selects those columns, so it 500s, and the saved-card flow — the highest-value
  thing shipped this week — **cannot be exercised on staging**. Fix, after the dump already taken at
  `/root/db-backups/nxeon_staging-pre-schema-sync-20260726-223109.sql`:
  `cd /opt/nxeon-staging && npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss`. The two unique constraints it
  adds are both safe here (`Mailbox` is empty; `stripePaymentIntentId` is a new all-NULL column) —
  see the callout at the top of this document.
- **The tree is behind production.** `docs/QA-JOURNEY.md:18-24` recorded staging 21 commits behind
  during the customer-journey rehearsal, which meant every finding had to be diffed against
  `/opt/nxeon` by hand before it could be claimed for production. *"The environment built to rehearse
  the release does not contain the release"* is itself a launch-readiness defect. Run
  `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` — which does the build, the `prisma db push` and the restarts — before
  trusting staging for anything.

```
  edit /opt/nxeon ──► git commit ──► post-commit hook auto-pushes to GitHub
                                        │
                      scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]
                                        │  build + prisma db push + restart staging
                                        ▼
                           verify on STAGING_HOST / :8080
                                        │
                      scripts/promote-production.sh
                                        │  rebuild + restart production
                                        ▼
                                      live
```

Domains and TLS are driven from **`/etc/nxeon/domains.env`** — currently `BASE_DOMAIN=nxeon.cloud`,
`ADMIN_HOST=4j3d7gkr2wcbi34.revsports.ca` (deliberately unguessable; `/admin` 404s on the customer
host), `STAGING_HOST=staging.revsports.ca`, plus `CERTBOT_EMAIL`. To move the platform to a new
domain: edit those four values, point DNS at the box, run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It
regenerates every vhost, obtains Let's Encrypt certificates, rewrites `APP_URL` in both `.env`
files, and restarts web. That is the whole migration.

this box, so the warnings are not decorative.

## Runbook — deploying a change

**Never build in the production tree while a background agent is also building it.** That race
corrupts `.next` output and has already caused a live styling outage.

```bash
# 1. Commit. The post-commit hook auto-pushes to GitHub.
cd /opt/nxeon
git status                      # confirm you know every changed file
git add -A && git commit -m "…"

# 2. Staging first.
/opt/nxeon/scripts/deploy-staging.sh            # or: deploy-staging.sh <ref>
#    builds + prisma db push + restarts nxeon-staging-web / -worker
curl -sI http://51.79.162.96:8080/ | head -1    # verify staging answers
journalctl -u nxeon-staging-worker -n 50 --no-pager

# 3. Promote.
/opt/nxeon/scripts/promote-production.sh        # rebuild + restart production

# 4. Verify.
systemctl is-active nxeon-web nxeon-worker
curl -sI https://nxeon.cloud/ | head -1
curl -s  https://nxeon.cloud/api/health
journalctl -u nxeon-worker -n 50 --no-pager
```

**Rules.**

I'm realizing staging deploys its own clone separately, so I need to figure out how to isolate the build directory there too while keeping the staging worker's source checkout intact and in sync.

Since both production and staging share the same deploy flow, I'm planning a shared library script parameterized by environment variables—repo dir, app dir, service names, ports, health check URLs, expected DB name, and deploy root—with thin env-specific wrappers calling into it.

I need to add retention and build configuration knobs like release count, build command, and dry-run/skip flags for testing scenarios, plus figure out how to resolve the target commit differently for each environment: production reads HEAD directly from its repo, while staging fetches origin and resolves a ref, so I need to check what staging's git remote actually points to before building the worktree-based build tree.

For production, I'll add a worktree off the main repo; for staging, a worktree off its own repo. The promotion flow still needs to verify staging's health on its port before promoting, and I want to keep that along with the static asset carry-over logic. I'm writing the health check polling loop...

For the health check itself, I'm having it extract the static JS chunk URL, verify it returns 200, confirm the build manifest for the new build ID is served (proving the deploy actually took), and check the public URL if configured. I'm debating adding `/api/health` as an additional default check path, but worried that could cause spurious rollbacks if it reflects unrelated subsystem degradation rather than the deploy itself -- leaning toward making the extra paths configurable rather than default.

For the restart step, I'm using systemctl to restart the web service and timing the downtime, with an eye toward how fast the Next.js standalone server actually boots. For rollback, I'm capturing the previous build target before the swap (via symlink or the renamed legacy directory) so that on health failure I can exchange it back into place and restore the prior working build.

I'm working out a generic swap/rollback helper that handles both symlink and real-directory cases, then restarts and checks health using the previous build's own BUILD_ID rather than the new one. I also want a state file tracking the current release and a deploy history log, plus a dedicated rollback script that locks, resolves the target release (previous or explicitly given), swaps it in, restarts, and re-verifies health.

For pruning, I'm deciding to keep the current release plus a fixed number of newest ones, always preserving current even if it's older after a rollback, and only clean up legacy directories once a later release has successfully promoted — on the very first migration there's nothing else to fall back to, so the legacy copy has to stay.

I should wrap all file manipulations in renames with an exit trap to clean up incoming leftovers, so the deployment never gets caught mid-state, and I need to think through what happens if the process dies right between the symlink swap and restart. For concurrency, I'll use a per-environment flock-based deploy lock that fails fast with the holding PID, plus a shared build lock to avoid redundant concurrent builds.

Now for prisma generate after the web cutover, I need to make sure it always runs with a clean environment pointed at the correct schema path, since the generated client bakes in the DATABASE_URL reference and I can't risk it picking up the wrong .env file.

So resolving to APP_DIR/.env — I need to verify this by checking the generated index.js for rootEnvPath and confirming it resolves correctly, plus confirm node_modules/.prisma and @prisma aren't symlinks in APP_DIR. I should also verify the build dir's client resolves to BUILD_DIR/.env with the expected DB, and the standalone copy's rootEnvPath resolves to standalone/.env matching APP_DIR/.env content, while making sure the build dir's node_modules are real rather than symlinked despite it being a git worktree.

For db push I'll use --skip-generate since I already generate the client explicitly beforehand. For the dry-run flow, I'm weighing whether to include a side-port smoke test running the new release on a spare port as the nxeon user against prod DB — but I'm uncertain whether the web app triggers background intervals like analytics flushes or chat agents on import, which makes that risky to claim is safe.

Actually I think running a side-port smoke test before every cutover, not just dry-runs, is the better approach since it catches boot crashes with zero downtime. I'm designing a PRESMOKE step that would use systemd-run to launch the standalone Next.js server as the nxeon user on a dedicated smoke port, loading the same environment file as production.

But I realize EnvironmentFile settings override Environment= settings in systemd, so the .env's PORT=3000 would clobber my smoke port override and collide with the live production port. I'm weighing alternatives like skipping EnvironmentFile entirely and instead loading a filtered env via a bash wrapper, though that risks shell-interpreting special characters in the .env values.

I'm fairly confident standalone's server.js does load .env files at startup, which is why Next copies them into the standalone output — so binding HOSTNAME to 127.0.0.1 keeps the smoke instance from being exposed externally, and the extra memory from a second Next instance should be negligible. Still, I want to double check whether Next actually reads .env in standalone mode, since if it doesn't, the smoke instance would be missing required config.

If it turns out Next doesn't load .env automatically, I'll fall back to parsing the .env file myself using Next's bundled @next/env package to extract the variables safely, testing this approach on staging first.
